articles.text: Get to know your candidates ahead of the November 5 election Each election cycle, the Piedmont Post provides extensive coverage of the city elections so that voters may learn about each candidate and make informed decisions on election day. In the weeks leading up to the November 5 election, we will continue to publish a regular Q&A segment in which candidates will answer questions about their background, qualifications and policies with a 200-word limit for each question. This week, the four candidates running for two seats on Piedmont’s City Council were asked to answer the following question: What inspired you to run for City Council? Conna McCarthy, Incumbent I am a candidate for re-election to City Council because I have the ability and experience to lead Piedmont through critical planning and management of our limited geographical and financial resources. Since joining Council in 2020, I have participated in ongoing discussions dealing with Piedmont’s aging infrastructure, state housing mandates, climate action, public safety, stewardship of our parks, and support for our schools. Prior to council, I served on the Recreation Commission and the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee. I’ve led successful parcel tax campaigns for both PUSD and the City. I know firsthand that community conversations among all stakeholders are critical to success. I believe in fair and transparent policies. I actively embrace inclusion. I believe public safety is paramount. I support highly trained, visible police officers who work to maintain safety while protecting civil rights. I support a highly trained fire department. I support Piedmont doing its part protecting the earth’s climate. My fiscal decisions respect the economic investment and personal sacrifices people make to live in Piedmont. I want Piedmont to be a place where our children want to raise their children and where newcomers from diverse backgrounds know they are welcome and wanted. Lorrel Plimier, Candidate I was inspired to run for City Council to continue to make a difference in my community, a commitment I’ve had since moving to Piedmont long before. I’m a military veteran and service has always been important to me. My husband grew up in Piedmont and when we moved to Piedmont with our young children, I was introduced to the strong volunteer culture here. I rolled up my sleeves and dug in to support my kids’ schools with my time, talents, and resources. After the 2016 election, I felt called to broaden my involvement beyond my kids’ schools. articles.text: Dear Friends and Colleagues: Please mark your calendar for September 19, 2024 at 6 pm. I’m reaching out to ask for your support in electing John Bauters as our next County Supervisor. Please join me at a special fundraiser at Chris Moore’s home at 431 Pacific Avenue in Piedmont. John Bauters is running against Oakland City Council President Nikki Fortunato Bas, whose failed policies have had a devastating impact on Oakland and indirectly Piedmont. Many voters may not realize that the Oakland Council President holds immense power, controlling the budget and shaping key policies. Under Nikki Bas’ leadership, Oakland has suffered from defunding the police (Nikki proposed a 50% cut), inaction on homelessness, the collapse of small businesses, and financial mismanagement that has brought the city to the brink of bankruptcy. Beholden to powerful unions, Nikki now wants to bring these disastrous policies to the county level, including her plans to divert funds from the County Sheriff to unproven alternatives. In contrast, John Bauters has a proven track record of effective leadership. As the former Mayor and City Council member of Emeryville, John has focused on supporting small businesses, add ressi ng homelessness, and prioritizing public safety. Emeryville may be smaller than Oakland, but it’s a model of thoughtful governance under John’s leadership. He has also served on multiple transportation committees and the Bay Area Air Quality Management District, showcasing his commitment to broader regional issues. You can learn more about John and his vision for our county at bautersforsupervisor.com. This fundraiser is independently organized and not directly connected to John’s campaign. All funds raised will support the independent expenditure committee “Bauters for a Safer East Bay,” with 100% of donations going towards educating voters on why John Bauters is the right choice for County Supervisor—and why Nikki Bas is not. Please join Chris Moore, Judy Cain, and many others to hear why we’re backing John Bauters and how you can help. We’re accepting donations as follows: RSVP to chrismoore@gmail. com You can donate now or at the event. We prefer donations by check: Bauters for a Safer East Bay 312 Clay Street, Suite 300 Oakland, CA 94607 Or you can donate online at efundraisingconnections.com/c/ Bauters. articles.text: Led by President Patty Dunlap, the new Board of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) recently met for the first meeting of its fiscal year. There was much to celebrate, as PBF has been serving the City of Piedmont for 60 years. PBF was formed in 1964 by an energetic group of members of the Piedmont Garden Club. The passage of Proposition 13 and other fiscal difficulties were causing Piedmont leaders to look at cutting funds for maintenance of the parks to assure adequate funding for Police and Fire. Because the funding was needed to preserve items the City had long paid for, it was thought an organization that partnered with the City would best serve the immediate and long-term needs. What was decided upon was an organization governed by eight Trustees, three appointed by the City Council and five by the Piedmont Garden Club. Typically, the Mayor, Vice Mayor and Chair of the Park Commission have been the City appointees. The Piedmont Garden Club Trustees have filled the officer positions. Many Advisors have completed the leadership ranks, including representatives from the other garden clubs in Piedmont. Dozens of projects located throughout the City have been completed over the last 60 years. Among the most memorable are the acquisition and installation of the Tea House near the Community Hall, the complete renovation of the area behind the Exedra, including installation of a fountain, and the acquisition of the Bufano Bears and renovation of Crocker Park. Perhaps most loved is the creation of a Holiday Tree – now part of the Lights Up! Ceremony – to illuminate Piedmont Park and usher in the winter holidays. PBF has been blessed with outstanding leadership throughout its 60 years. Presidents typically serve for two years. Remarkably, seven members now serving on its current Board are past presidents. This has provided marvelous continuity and support for the current leadership. There can be little doubt the new group of PBF leaders were fully justified in raising a glass of Champagne to toast the last 60 years. Watch for the year-end brochure which will highlight possible projects for the future. Love is the currency of humanity...spend lavishly. Beautification Foundation begins its 60th year of serving the city of Piedmont.

articles.text: Annual music festival in its 23rd year The 23rd Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival will take place in Piedmont Main Park on Sunday, September 22. The event is free to the public. The first performers will take the stage beginning at 11:00 a.m. This city-sponsored event occurs in conjunction with the annual Piedmont Harvest Festival. “It’s a celebration of the musical talent of Piedmont,” explained the festival’s longtime organizer, Greg Slatoff. Opening the festival will be Carlos Caminos, a local jazz-flamenco fusion guitarist originally from Venezuela. “He’s going to open the show with an acoustic set that should be more calm and even,” said Slatoff. “We don’t want to blast the city awake at 11 o’clock in the morning.” Next, the Piedmont High School Jazz Band will perform under the direction of new PHS Band director Trevor Messeroll. A graduate of Berklee College of Music, he took over the role in September 2023 after the departure of longtime PHS band director Andria Mullan. The Puckett Family Project will be the penultimate act of the festival. Originally started in 1998 as a solo project by frontman and Piedmont resident Tod Puckett, the band, now with nine members, is known for its high-energy brand of Americana rock and funk. The band has shared bills with a wide range of bands including Ricky Skaggs, Tea Leaf Green, Acoustic Junction and The Will Bernard Trio. The band also recently released its fifth album, No Invite, now available on Spotify and Apple Music. Closing the afternoon will be a five-piece tango band, Molinete, playing mostly original pieces in their unique blend of Argentinian tango and jazz. The band’s name is a Spanish word meaning “to spin or twist one thing around a pivot point” – a concept the band said is a fundamental dance element of tango. The festival is scheduled to finish around 3:00 p.m. For more information about the Jazz Festival, contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@yahoo.com. 11:00 – 12:00 12:00 – 1:00 1:30 – 2:15 2:15 – 3:00 Molinete

articles.text: As the summer winds down and fall nears, this year’s 9th grade Girl Scouts are working hard to finish their Silver Award projects, and Rose Reining and Olivia Bailey are ahead of the game. Their Silver Award project is a website focused on pet adoption and care for anyone who needs it. “Our goal is to facilitate pet ownership and make helpful resources accessible to all” explained Olivia Bailey. Their website has three main sections. The first section focuses on disabled animals, the second is about old and sick animals, and the third section details the supplies and resources necessary for pet ownership. But what is a Silver Award project? “I like to compare it to an Eagle Scout project,” said Rose Reining. “The Girl Scout equivalent of an Eagle Scout award is a Gold Award, and the Silver Award is one step below that.” Silver Awards projects are designed to make a lasting impact and help solve an issue in the community. Scouts are required to spend a minimum of 50 hours on their Silver Award projects, though most end up taking more time to produce work of higher quality. “We are helping to prevent food waste by connecting home gardens to foodbanks,” said Girl Scout Mina Herrgott. Other projects being done by Girl Scout Troop 33521 include brochures to assist immigrants, murals and making films. To visit Rose and Olivia’s website, go to tinyurl.com/PetAdoptAndCare To learn more about Mina Hergott and Audrey Levin’s project, see tinyurl.com/FoodWasteBrochure
articles.title: Bailey, Reining plan for Girl Scout Silver Award

In celebration of Hispanic Heritage Month, the public is invited to a day-long celebration featuring guest speaker Dr. Jessica Marquez, a NASA Ames engineer who will speak about space. Since 2007, Dr. Marquez has been working at the NASA Ames Research Center within the Human Systems Integration Division. As part of the Human-Computer Interaction Group, she has supported the development and deployment of planning and scheduling software tools for various space missions, including the International Space Station Program. She now leads the team that is developing Playbook, a web-based planning, scheduling, and execution software tool. Her work has led to supporting different NASA analog missions that simulate planetary missions and spacewalks. Dr. Marquez also is a subject matter expert for space human factors engineering, specifically in human-automation-robotic integration. The day also features activities including bilingual storytime featuring the inspiring stories of Ellen Ochoa’s Journey to the Moon and The Boy Who Touched the Stars. Make-your-own bold and eccentric jewelry with Bianquis, a Chicana jewelry designer and artist native to the East Bay who has been creating stunning work from upcycled materials and more recently, working with clay to make objects that reflect her Mexican heritage. In addition, Chabot will present a full schedule of planetarium shows and resources tabling with partners from the Latinx community. articles.text: Piedmont Cub Scouts in Pack 3 gathered for a ceremony to formally begin their Scouting year on the 23rd anniversary of 9/11. articles.text: Friday night’s football game was a one-sided affair in Piedmont High’s third game of the season, shutting out the visiting Mt. Eden Monarchs 35-0 under the lights at Witter Field on Friday, September 13. It wasn’t the fastest start for the Highlanders in a scoreless he first quarter and relinquishing its opening two possessions without a score before breaking the deadlock late in the second quarter. “I kind of had a feeling we would come out slow. A football saying is, ‘You can’t play with your food.’ Mt. Eden played hard, but we’ve dominated this team in our last two meetings. When you get used to that, it can make people lackadaisical a bit. It was just a sloppy start but we cleaned things up,” coach Jordan Seiden said. Piedmont’s defenders were in Mt. Eden’s backfield frequently for the entire night, recording 11 tackles for loss. Inside linebacker Cash Elmquist wreaked havoc on the Monarchs, constantly lining up over center and shooting between Mt. Eden’s offensive line. “We were confident coming in but we weren’t happy with that first quarter. We changed up a little with five down linemen and our defense just started eating; a lot of tackles for loss and almost had a couple of interceptions,” Elmquist said. One new player, Xavier Anderson, has also made an impact on both sides of the ball. The junior transferred to Piedmont from Oakland Tech, lining up at outside linebacker, running back, and can reel in a reception as a receiver—recording his first touchdown for Piedmont. Xavier Anderson tackles a Mt. Eden running back for a loss. Quarterback Markos Lagios flattens a Mt. Eden defender with a stiff-arm. Linebacker Cash Elmquist led the team with 11 tackles. Staff Photos “We started a little slow, but coach had some words in the locker room that fired us up. We just had to come out and execute. But that was my first touchdown in the ‘P’; it feels great, I love it. I’m happy to be here, it’s a great culture,” Anderson said. Piedmont has two games left in its pre-league schedule – Encinal this Friday and Dougherty Valley on October 4, both at home. Seiden knows it’s important for PHS to remain healthy before taking on its Mission Division competition in the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont’s schedule with league teams starts October 11 at Hayward. “We need to just stay healthy. That’s not to say we’re overlooking anyone, but we know we have to stay healthy over a full season to compete for league and NCS,” Seiden said. Game Recap Piedmont and Mt. Eden ended the first quarter in a 0-0 tie, but the Highlanders got rolling in the second quarter and held a 14-0 lead at halftime. PHS scored three touchdowns in the third quarter to put the game out of reach at 35-0. Both teams traded possession until Piedmont assumed a short field at the Mt. Eden 32 following a botched punt in the second quarter. PHS scored in seven plays to make it 7-0 with 4:53 left in the first half when quarterback Markos Lagios scored on a fouryear touchdown run. PHS forced a punt on Mt. Eden’s next series then scored after just five plays on a 55-yard drive. It started with a big 26 yard carry by Lagios, then hit Shelby on a pair of 13-yard gains. Tommy Ashton then ran the ball into the end zone on a five-yard carry with 1:32 on the clock. Piedmont started with the ball in the third quarter, scoring on a 70-yard series of plays within three minutes. It started with a 24 yard carry by Ashton, then Shelby had receptions of 25 and 18 yards to make it 1st-and-Goal at the five. At the one-yard line, Lagios found Anderson on a play-action pass—21-0 with 9:10 on the clock. The Highlanders’ next touchdown came on just one play, where Shelby took a reception 77 yards to the house to make it 28-0 with 7:17 left in the third. On the play, Shelby initially caught the ball on the left side, switching the field to sprint down the right sideline into the end zone. After another Mt. Eden punt, Piedmont scored its final touchdown with 2:16 left in the third on a 10-play, three minute series. They capped it off on Lagios’ second touchdown run, this time on a four-yard scamper. Final stats: Lagios completed 12-19 passes for 208 yards and two touchdowns, to go along with 44 rushing yards and another two touchdowns. Ashton had 61 rushing yards on 12 carries and a touchdown. Shelby had 10 receptions for 202 yards and a touchdown, to go along with 29 rushing yards on three attempts. Anderson had one touchdown. Defensively, Elmquist had three tackles for loss and a pass defense. Jordan Alemania also had three tackles for loss. Anderson, Rehan Mumtaz, Nick King, Brandon Dicke, and Bill Ashton also had individual tackles for loss. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-1) hosts Encinal at Witter Field this Friday, September 20 at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Fencing Team traveled to Italy and England as they trained for the upcoming season. The squad gets started this month. Piedmont Fencing Team is returns from the offseason and begins its 2024-25 season. The team’s long, grueling season runs from September to the National Championships in early July. During the offseason coach David Sinkkonen and his athletes traveled to Italy and England for their annual overseas training sessions. In Italy, the squad had the unique experience of training with Olympic silver medalist, Filippo Macchi. “We did a camp in Florence, Italy run by Marco Vannini, who is an Olympic coach. It was an excellent camp with kids from all around the world. Marco’s main student, Filippo Macchi, helped train students. Filippo won two silver medals at the Olympics. He won his second silver right before the camp started. He was just one touch from being an Olympic champion,” Sinkkonen said. The team then trained in England for Sinkkonen’s own fencing camp. PFT found a new athlete during their time overseas, Nathaniel Goff. Even though Piedmont senior Oliver Greenebaum (left) enters a critical year as a leader. Goff, 16, resides in the UK, he is able to represent Piedmont when he competes in the United States. “Nathaniel is one of our Piedmont fencers but lives in the UK. Our group has kids from UK and France as well. He’s located in London but fences in tournaments in the U.S. ,” Sinkkonen said. Two of Piedmont Fencing Maya Dvoiris (right) is a Piedmont Middle School eighth grader competing with the Piedmont Fencing Team. Team’s athletes get their season started this weekend on Saturday and Sunday, September 21-22. Piedmont Middle School 8th grader Maya Dvoiris will compete at the Battle in Space City Regional Open Circuit in Houston, and Asher Aguilar of Beach School will travel to Torrance in Southern California for the 12th Annual Little Musketeers RJC. Dvoiris is set to compete in three events, including Cadet Women’s Foil, Division 2 Women’s Foil, and Junior Women’s Foil. Aguilar will compete in the Youth 10 Men’s Foil. “Maya is someone to keep an eye on, she just has to fix some things and if she does, she’ll be really successful. Asher is competing in the Youth 10 category and has a lot of potential. We’re keeping an eye on both of them,” Sinkkonen said. Piedmont’s first full event comes on September 28-29 at the Air Force ROC/RJCC in Colorado Springs. The team will be represented by Goff in four events, by Kulkarni in four events, and by Piedmont High senior Oliver Greenebaum.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team extended its winless streak to seven matches after falling 3-0 to Berean Christian on Thursday, September 12 at Binks Rawlings Gym. The Eagles entered Piedmont as defending North Coast Section champion, and with a current record of 12-3 are well on their way to repeat. Piedmont, meanwhile, is a young team looking for its first win. PHS had a close second set against Berean, but ended up losing the match in three sets,: 25-16, 25-21, 25-14. “We’re a young team; I’m going to say that a lot this season. We’re going to have some tough matches, but we have glimpses of our potential,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Piedmont looks ahead to its first match in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division next week on September 25 against Alameda. Match Recap After falling 25-16 in the first set, Piedmont got out to an early 4-1 lead in the second. However, BC scored six straight points to jump ahead 7-4. From there, PHS crept back to ties at 8-8 and 10-10, including two aces by Fiona Olsen and kills by Hanley Carling and Stella Wilk. However, the Eagles went up 13-11 and never relinquished their advantage from then on. PHS traded shots with Berean Christian, getting within two points of tying multiple times until the end of the second set. PHS made it 16-14 with a kill by Carling, but BCHS scored three straight after that. Piedmont then scored three consecutive to make it 19-17 with kills by Carling and Olsen, but the Eagles scored three out of the next four. After a kill by Mira Sachs and an ace by Jules DeYoung cut the deficit to 22-20, Berean Christian scored another two, gaining set-point at 24-20. An Eagles service error made it 24-21, but the visitors ended it with a spike. In the third set, the Eagles came out firing with six straight points to build a comfortable 6-0 lead. PHS battled to an 8-4 deficit with an ace by Skye Prata and a kill by Carling, but BCHS scored eight of the next 11 points to build a 16-6 advantage. The two sides traded points until the 25-14 end. articles.text: Over the summer, Todd Sullivan announced his resignation as Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer coach after eight years at the helm. He concludes his time at the school with 87 wins in 155 total matches, accumulating Division 2 North Coast Section titles in 2023 and 2022, along with Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division titles in 2019, 2021 and 2022. With Sullivan departing from the school as Piedmont’s all-time most successful soccer coach, we take a look back at his time as head coach. Prior to Sullivan’s arrival in the Sullivan winter of 2016/2017, Piedmont went 8-8-8 under Rory O’Connor. After four years under O’Connor, could only muster one NCS win. PHS finished 9-2-9 (W-T-L) Sullivan’s first year and 7-2-13 his second year in 2018. Then, in 2019, everything changed. Going into the 2019, Sullivan talked about changing Piedmont’s style of play from a direct, “bomb it long” type of approach into a highly-possessive team that provides a lot of pressure for all 80 minutes of regulation. In 2019, Piedmont went 12-2-5 overall and undefeated 9-1-0 in league to claim the Shoreline banner. PHS won the Shoreline on a cold and rainy February 1 night with a 1-0 win over Hayward—marking Piedmont’s first league title in 10 years. On that 2009 title team was the school’s all-time leading goal scorer, Nikolai Littleton, as an assistant coach. At the time, he proclaimed that Piedmont soccer was back on the map. Littleton was a part of a 21-2-3 squad, which made it to the Semifinals of the North Coast Section 2A Playoffs in 2009. Little did Nikolai know just how right he was. “It’s crazy how life comes full circle,” said Littleton in 2019. “My junior-year team was a great team, and since then there hasn’t been a lot of success – until now. I think this shows that Piedmont soccer is back. These guys proved it.” After falling short of a second straight Shoreline title in 2020, Piedmont returned from the pandemic for its shortened season in the spring of 2021. They went undefeated against other league teams to go 10-0-0 with its only loss against Foothill team, Bishop O’Dowd. The 2022 Piedmont team was a team on a mission. They finished the season with a 15-2-4 overall record and 13-0-3 in league to finish atop the Shoreline for a third consecutive year and a subsequent promotion to the Foothill Division. It was a season that culminated in the school’s first-ever D2 NCS championship. On a cold February 26 night, Piedmont’s No. 1 seeded team won 1-0 over No. 2 University at Witter Field. In the 67th minute, former captain Andre Stankiewicz slotted in the game-winner after rebounding his own shot off of the keeper. “Cameones! Campeones! Ole, ole, ole!” rang from Piedmont’s locker room after the historic win. Piedmont’s NCS title in 2022 Todd Sullivan left Piedmont High School as the school’s all-time most decorated soccer coach. The Matchbox Magic Flute is Zimmerman’s adaptation of Mozart’s iconic opera Magic Flute, using only 10 singers and five musicians. The adaption reimagines Mozart’s beloved opera by using big music in a small space with a few talented artists and actors. “Berkeley Rep is my theatrical home away from home,” said Zimmerman. “It was the first theatre ever to produce a run of a show of mine outside of Chicago, and it remains my favorite place to come. I love the theatre, the entire staff, the audiences, and the surrounding city, hills, and Bay. The whole cast is really excited to spend time here with our crazy little music-hall Flute.” The cast of The Matchbox Magic Flute includes Marlene Fernandez, Emilie Lynn, Russell Mernagh, Lauren Molina, Tina Muñoz-Pandya, Reese Parish, Shawn Pfautsch, Emily Rohm, Billy Rude and Monica West. The play runs through December 8. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/the-matchbox-magic-flute/. From the Goodman Theatre production of The Matchbox Magic Flute

articles.text: Festival Opera’s 33rd season will continue into autumn with a trio of Sunday afternoon artist recitals at the intimate Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series will launch on Sunday, September 22, at 4 p.m. with Lucky in Love presenting mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and Piedmont favorite, pianist Jeffrey LaDeur, founder of San Francisco International Piano Festival The series will continue on Sunday, October 27, at 4 p.m. with Nothing to Fear featuring contralto Sara Couden and pianist Derek Tam. The final recital will be on Sunday, November 17 at 4 p.m. with Muses and Musings of an Impresario – a birthday celebration with special guest artists to be announced – showcasing Festival Opera General Director and baritone Zachary Gordin as well as pianist Daniel Lockert. Sunday, Sept. 22 at 4 p.m. Lucky in Love According to Kindra Scharich, “Lucky in Love celebrates the centennial anniversary of legendary French composer Gabriel Fauré by highlighting one of his most important song cycles: La Bonne Chanson. Inspired by his passionate love for soprano Emma Bardac and based on the exquisite poetry of Paul Verlaine, Fauré called La Bonne Chanson his “most exuberant writing.” Mezzo-soprano Kindra Scharich and pianist Jeffrey LaDeur present this work, alongside other beloved scores that explore l’amour! Sunday, Oct. 27 at 4 p.m. Nothing to Fear Contralto Sara Couden commented, “What do art, song and Halloween have in common? Well…monsters. Beasts without and within, love gone horribly wrong, generalized anxiety and existential crises, conversations with death… the world of classical music is rife with horrors, and I am excited to introduce as many of them as possible to the audience this October. I will be working with the fabulous and multi-talented pianist Derek Tam and presenting works by a list of composers including Schubert, Strauss, Wieck and Weill as well as modern composers Jordan Rutter-Covatto, Erika Oba and Chris Castro. Don’t worry, there’s nothing to fear… but fear (/love/ death/the beast within) itself.” Sunday, Nov. 17 at 4 p.m. Muses and Musings of an Impresario Baritone Zachary Gordin said, “I am honored to collaborate with this group of Bay Area treasures on this recital series and most especially to rekindle my work with the incomparable Daniel Lockert in a recital of repertoire and anecdotes that will tell a story of my journey and muses in this life of music. Songs of composers so very dear to me [will be featured]: Schumann, Mahler, Reynaldo Hahn and Jake Heggie mixed with a splash of early music and American Songbook classics.” Surprise guests are to be announced, and a birthday celebration reception including wine, bubbly and treats will follow the program. Tickets for the Festival Opera Artist Recital Series at the Piedmont Center for the Arts are $40 per person for each concert, or individuals may purchase all programs for the discounted price of $95. To purchase tickets online, visit www.festivalopera.org.

articles.text: Piedmont artist Larraine Seiden will display her work at the 50th annual San Francisco Open Studios (SFOS) on October 5 and 6 from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. It will be her 20th appearance at the Open Studios exhibit. Seiden, who teaches art at Wildwood School, has faithfully participated in SFOS since 2003 and credits Artspan, the local nonprofit that runs the event, with her artistic development. “The only times I missed it were in 2006 and 2008 due to the births of my kids,” said Seiden. San Francisco Open Studios is a citywide open studio exhibition that takes place over four weekends in the fall each year. Started in 1975, the event highlights a different city district each weekend. In 2023, over 600 local artists participated in SFOS, according to news site Mission Local. The theme this year is “From Disco Days to the Tech Craze,” a nostalgic nod to the way the nonprofit has supported a continuous arts community through San Francisco’s many ups and downs over the past 50 years. In 2020, organizers even took SFOS online when COVID-19 restrictions made in-person gatherings difficult to plan. For Seiden, this will be her first time showing at the event’s design district showroom. For the last two decades, Seiden has had a close relationship with Artspan and SFOS. When she finished graduate school, Artspan was the organization she counted on for support in showing her early paintings and sculptures around San Francisco. Advocating for community through creativity is a vital priority for Seiden, who is a founding board member of Piedmont Makers. In 2020, she co-founded the Piedmont Artwalk with Jon Schleuning as a fundraiser for the Piedmont Arts Fund. Later that year, Seiden was asked by Artspan to join the Open Studios Committee, a role she still serves in today, where she encourages emerging artists to get involved in the San Francisco art scene. Seiden’s painting Seamless #14 is featured in Artspan’s publicity poster for the event. Her work can also be viewed in the SFOS 2024 catalogs which let readers preview hundreds of artists and plan their visits for each of the event’s four weekends. SFOS catalogs are free and can be found on Mulberry’s news racks while supplies last. Visit Larraine and 12 other artists during SF Open Studios October 5-6 at Room & Board’s San Francisco showroom, 685 7th Street. Free parking will be available on-site. articles.text: The Piedmont Post is presenting one month of reviews of films by celebrated Japanese animation director, Hayao Miyazaki. As a writer, director, and animator he is one of the most revered filmmakers in Japan, and worldwide. His award-wining animated films have been embraced by audiences that have found his beautifully detailed hand-drawn visuals and thematic storytelling compelling. As well, his protagonists are often strong young girls or resilient young women. Miyazaki co-founded the now iconic Studio Ghibli in 1985. In 2012 he was named a Person of Cultural Merit for his outstanding cultural contributions. He received an Academy Honorary Award for his impact on animation and cinema in 2014. His work continues to serve as an inspiration for countless animators, directors and writers. This week’s reviews are: Ponyo (2008) and Howl’s Moving Castle (2004). How to view Within a very short period, streaming has all but revolutionized what was once simply referred to as “going to the movies.” Films that were released in theaters for a limited time and often missed are now available. If your youngster missed, say, Studio Ghibli’s Oscar-winning Spirited Away (2001), it is now available. Also Pixar’s first or second Toy Story, or their acclaimed Inside Out. All that’s required is a television or a subscription to Prime, Netflix, or Disney+. Hayao Miyazaki

articles.text: Howl’s Moving Castle represents another tour de force from the extraordinary imagination of writer-director Hayao Miyazaki and the Japanese animation Studio Ghibli. Adapted from the novel by Diana Wynne Jones, it is set in Europe and features an 18-year-old girl, Sophie (Emily Mortimer), a shy young hat maker, who is transformed into a 90-year-old woman (Jean Simmons) by the jealous Wicked Witch of the Waste (Lauren Bacall). Looking in the mirror Sophie is shocked to see a stooped and gnarled old woman and it becomes her quest to somehow break the Witch’s spell. Unexpectedly she meets an attractive, inscr utable, shape-shifting Wizard, Howl (Christian Bale), who lives in a mobile, steampunkish, labyrinthine four-legged castle. But, of course, this is a Miyazaki tale and Sophie’s adventure soon veers off in unexpected directions, involving a war, a fire demon (Billy Crystal), and even a silent, sentient scarecrow. As well, unlike many of Hollywood’s films aimed at a younger audience, Miyazaki does not draw deep lines between good and evil, often seeming more comfortable with the ambiguous. For example, the Wizard can seem both malicious and benign; Sophie comes to care for the Witch who cast the transformative spell; and with regards to war, it’s never clear what side should prevail. The story also seems to ask the question whether war is not only futile but also an absurd human endeavor. All of the above is framed by understated humor and a sense of floating animé, which is vibrant, engaging, and filled with wonder. Note: For very young children Howl’s Moving Castle may be too intense with a plot that may be difficult to follow. Howl’s Moving Castle. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. From Studio Ghibli. Voiced by Emily Mortimer, Billy Crystal, Jean Simmons, Lauren Bacall and Christian Bale. 2 hrs. Rated: PG. Streaming on MAX/ prime/Fandango/HULU/apple tv.
articles.title: Howl’s Moving Castle a tour de force

articles.text: Ponyo, written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki, is a visual treat, displaying a hand-drawn style that is reminiscent of early Disney, the colors vibrant while creating a soft, less delineated, yet pleasing effect. Ultimately, however, the success of Ponyo for an American audience, rests with its narrative. At its center, the film is a love story between a young boy, Sosuke (Frankie Jonas), and a small fish, Ponyo (Noah Cyrus). When Sosuke rescues Ponyo from the sea (she is trapped in a glass jar), she falls in love with him and wills herself to become human. Her decision has countless unintended consequences, involving her father, Fujimoto (Liam Neeson), a King Neptune of sorts, and her mother, Gran Mamare (Cate Blanchett). And so the film spins off into a tsunami-like storm that results in Sosuke setting out, with Ponyo, to find his mother (Tina Fey). While Disney enthusiastically promoted Ponyo to American audiences as an animated feature, it is a much different film than Disney customarily produces. It is different in tone and dialogue from the signature Disneyesque fare. In Japan, animation, also known as animé, is not just the province of children. Adults are completely taken with the genre, as they are with manga, which are illustrated stories, drawn in black and white. Manga comics can look like phone books, can be lengthy serials, and are read intensely by a broad spectrum of Japanese society. It is likely that Miyazaki had two audiences in mind when he wrote and directed Ponyo, resulting in a story that seems ultimately more slated for an older audience than children ages 6 to 9. But like most children’s films it does end with a moral – value loyalty, love and family above all else. Ponyo. Directed and illustrated by Hayao Miyazaki. Voiced by Noah Cyrus, Liam Neeson, Cate Blanchett. Animation by Studio Ghibli. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated G. Released in 2019. Streaming on Fandango/prime/ MAX/apple tv. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Ponyo

articles.text: A group of 22 book lovers showed up on September 9 for the First Monday Reading Group’s discussion of The Heaven and Earth Grocery Store by James McBride, released in 2023 to favorable reviews. The novel starts in 1972 in Pottstown, Pennsylvania, where an excavation operation for a new housing complex discovers a skeleton in the bottom of a well. Some items are found near the body, including a mezuza, which leads a policeman to question the town’s only Jewish resident. However, the investigation is hampered when the crime scene is washed away by Hurricane Agnes. The story then goes back to the 1920s and 30s and details the lives of the town’s residents in what was mostly the Black and Jewish Chicken Hill neighborhood. Two of the Jewish residents, husband and wife Moshe and Chona Ludlow, own a local theater with a dance hall and The Heaven & Earth Grocery Store. Nate Timblin, one of the town’s Black residents who works for the Ludlows, asks them to hide a deaf young Black boy, Dodo, from the authorities who are trying to institutionalize him in a notorious mental asylum. The actions of the town physician, who is a member of the Ku Klux Klan and has sexual desires for Chona, lead to Dodo being sent to the asylum. The Black and Jewish townspeople mobilize to help the boy. The book provided a lot of enjoyment for the readers; McBride is a wonderful storyteller. It was “a large book with more than a touch of Charles Dickens” said one reader. There are multiple layers to the story. The themes of communities working and living together, the importance of families, and how people are treated all resonated with the readers. McBride took his time developing the characters and provided details that most readers enjoyed. However for other readers felt the characters were stereotypes or caricatures. The stereotypes had some truth to them and these readers could relate to them. This was especially true for readers who had personal experiences with the setting, or the Jewish, Black, and disabled communities. McBride seemed to be poking fun at everyone. The readers were emotionally touched by the harsh treatment of Dodo and his severely handicapped asylum friend, Monkey Pants. Readers could feel for the characters who didn’t have a lot of love in their lives. The group also liked the strong women who drove the story’s action. Pleasure was taken by the justice rendered to the bad guys and the story’s mostly happy ending. Objections from the were that more than a half of the book was a “slog” with too many characters and too many details. The book needed a better editor, they felt, and an important story was being treated in a slapstick manner. Some other interesting, related elements emerged from the discussion too. The characters had a distrust of the area’s government and its ability to perform basic functions. This may have contributed to the development of the Mafia. The readers had previously selected Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell for their October book and North Woods by Danile Mason for November. After hearing reviews presented by Laura Goldman of three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected Leadership: In Turbulent Times by Doris Kearns Goodwin for their December read. The group’s next discussion will be on October 7 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join and there is no fee. Register at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group was up for a longer walk last week on a lovely morning with a strong turnout of 50 walkers and one K-9 best friend. St. James Drive is a long, flat street and easy to walk. Going all the way to its end at Park Boulevard would let the walkers see a very little visited street with Piedmont homes, Cavendish Lane. There were places along the way to turn back for anyone not wanting to go this far. The group went up Crocker Avenues to Hampton Road and the beginning of St. James Drive. Two white columns mark one of the entrances to St. James Woods, a very large real estate development begun in the 1920s. The neighborhood was governed by the St. James Wood Homes Association founded in 1926 and represents over 185 homes in Piedmont and Oakland. The CC&Rs have some restrictions on what homeowners can do with their property. However, the last annual meeting and website posting was in 2012. Phil Witte, who lives on St. James Drive, said the association is no longer active. The columns are missing lanterns on their tops. The neighborhood once wanted the City to put replicas of the originals on them, but neither the residents nor the City wanted to pay for them, so it never happened. The walkers also noted the distinctive four brown tiles that are inlayed in each section of all the concrete sidewalks that were part of this neighborhood. St. James is seven tenths of a mile long to its end at Park Blvd. At St. James’ end just past Trestle Glen Road is Cavendish Lane, a narrow street that looks like an alley. It is in Oakland, but there are four homes with Piedmont addresses at its end. The street was damaged in February 2017 after it was undermined by heavy rains and a construction project on a Trestle Glen home below. The hillside and road slipped away, and the Piedmont families were unable to access their homes by car for six weeks. The City of Piedmont made temporary fixes, but permanent repairs by Oakland did not begin until 2019, two years later due to inaction by the City of Oakland. After walking a few hundred feet the group saw the repaired roadway, a retaining wall, and the hillside below with rusting concrete rebar on top of it. A hard-to-read Piedmont Public Works notice, dated August 2021, was taped on the wall and said all construction work was to be stopped because of violations of City ordinances. It seemed that nothing had been done to the hillside since the walkers’ visit last year. The group retraces their steps back to the middle of town, It had been a four-mile walk, longer than usual. Walkers explore the length of St. James Dr. By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group was up for a longer walk last week on a lovely morning with a strong turnout of 50 walkers and one K-9 best friend. St. James Drive is a long, flat street and easy to walk. Going all the way to its end at Park Boulevard would let the walkers see a very little visited street with Piedmont homes, Cavendish Lane. There were places along the way to turn back for anyone not wanting to go this far. The group went up Crocker Avenues to Hampton Road and the beginning of St. James Drive. Two white columns mark one of the entrances to St. James Woods, a very large real estate development begun in the 1920s. The neighborhood was governed by the St. James Wood Homes Association founded in 1926 and represents over 185 homes in Piedmont and Oakland. The CC&Rs have some restrictions on what homeowners can do with their property. However, the last annual meeting and website posting was in 2012. Phil Witte, who lives on St. James Drive, said the association is no longer active. The columns are missing lanterns on their tops. The neighborhood once wanted the City to put replicas of the originals on them, but neither the residents nor the City wanted to pay for them, so it never happened. The walkers also noted the distinctive four brown tiles that are inlayed in each section of all the concrete sidewalks that were part of this neighborhood. St. James is seven tenths of a mile long to its end at Park Blvd. At St. James’ end just past Trestle Glen Road is Cavendish Lane, a narrow street that looks like an alley. It is in Oakland, but there are four homes with Piedmont addresses at its end. The street was damaged in February 2017 after it was undermined by heavy rains and a construction project on a Trestle Glen home below. The hillside and road slipped away, and the Piedmont families were unable to access their homes by car for six weeks. The City of Piedmont made temporary fixes, but permanent repairs by Oakland did not begin until 2019, two years later due to inaction by the City of Oakland. After walking a few hundred feet the group saw the repaired roadway, a retaining wall, and the hillside below with rusting concrete rebar on top of it. A hard-to-read Piedmont Public Works notice, dated August 2021, was taped on the wall and said all construction work was to be stopped because of violations of City ordinances. It seemed that nothing had been done to the hillside since the walkers’ visit last year. The group retraces their steps back to the middle of town, It had been a four-mile walk, longer than usual. First Monday Reading Group discusses Heaven and Earth By Dick Carter A group of 22 book lovers showed up on September 9 for the First Monday Reading Group’s discussion of The Heaven and Earth Grocery Store by James McBride, released in 2023 to favorable reviews. The novel starts in 1972 in Pottstown, Pennsylvania, where an excavation operation for a new housing complex discovers a skeleton in the bottom of a well. Some items are found near the body, including a mezuza, which leads a policeman to question the town’s only Jewish resident. However, the investigation is hampered when the crime scene is washed away by Hurricane Agnes. The story then goes back to the 1920s and 30s and details the lives of the town’s residents in what was mostly the Black and Jewish Chicken Hill neighborhood. Two of the Jewish residents, husband and wife Moshe and Chona Ludlow, own a local theater with a dance hall and The Heaven & Earth Grocery Store. Nate Timblin, one of the town’s Black residents who works for the Ludlows, asks them to hide a deaf young Black boy, Dodo, from the authorities who are trying to institutionalize him in a notorious mental asylum. The actions of the town physician, who is a member of the Ku Klux Klan and has sexual desires for Chona, lead to Dodo being sent to the asylum. The Black and Jewish townspeople mobilize to help the boy. The book provided a lot of enjoyment for the readers; McBride is a wonderful storyteller. It was “a large book with more than a touch of Charles Dickens” said one reader. There are multiple layers to the story. The themes of communities working and living together, the importance of families, and how people are treated all resonated with the readers. McBride took his time developing the characters and provided details that most readers enjoyed. However for other readers felt the characters were stereotypes or caricatures. The stereotypes had some truth to them and these readers could relate to them. This was especially true for readers who had personal experiences with the setting, or the Jewish, Black, and disabled communities. McBride seemed to be poking fun at everyone. The readers were emotionally touched by the harsh treatment of Dodo and his severely handicapped asylum friend, Monkey Pants. Readers could feel for the characters who didn’t have a lot of love in their lives. The group also liked the strong women who drove the story’s action. Pleasure was taken by the justice rendered to the bad guys and the story’s mostly happy ending. Objections from the were that more than a half of the book was a “slog” with too many characters and too many details. The book needed a better editor, they felt, and an important story was being treated in a slapstick manner. Some other interesting, related elements emerged from the discussion too. The characters had a distrust of the area’s government and its ability to perform basic functions. This may have contributed to the development of the Mafia. The readers had previously selected Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell for their October book and North Woods by Danile Mason for November. After hearing reviews presented by Laura Goldman of three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected Leadership: In Turbulent Times by Doris Kearns Goodwin for their December read. articles.text: Dear MacMama: I see there is a new iPhone out. I have an iPhone 12, should I upgrade? There seem to be so many choices, can you explain? –Lizzy, Piedmont Dear Lizzy: Every year around the middle of September, Apple comes out with a new iPhone. Soon to follow that is a new operating system for the iPhone and iPads. And every year the speed gets better the camera gets better, and hopefully the battery gets better although that hasn’t always been the case. If you are a person who likes to travel and uses your iPhone to take pictures then I would say absolutely, it’s a great idea to upgrade to the new iPhone 16. Of course there are actually four versions of the iPhone 16. There’s the iPhone 16, the 16 Plus, the 16 Pro and the 16 Pro Max. The features between the models and their respective larger versions are not very different, but there are notable differences between the iPhone 16 models and the more expensive and feature-rich Pro models. These are all available for order and will be in stock as of Sept. 20. iPhone 16 and 16 Plus: The iPhone 16 has a 6.1-inch display and is the smallest iPhone 16 available. The 16 Plus model has a 6.7 inch display. These iPhones have an aluminum case with a color infused glass back and come in five colors including ultramarine, teal, pink, white and black. The cameras on these models are what Apple calls the Advanced dual-camera system 48MP Fusion 12MP Ultra Wide. They have optical zoom capability at .5, 1x and 2x. This is a much more advanced camera than your iPhone 12 has, but not as advanced as the pro models of the iPhone 16. The iPhone 16 comes in three storage capacity choices; 128 GB for $799, 256 GB for $899 or 512 GB for $1099. The iPhone 16 plus has the same storage capacity choices and is $100 more expensive for each iPhone 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max The Pro models are slightly bigger. The iPhone 16 Pro has a 6.3 inch display, while the 16 Pro Max has a 6.9 inch display. These models have a titanium case with textured matt glass back. They come in four colors; desert titanium, natural titanium, white and black. It’s with the camera on the pro models that we start to see some of the major differences of the pro models to the less expensive iPhone 16 models. In these phones, Apple has included what they call the Pro camera system with 48MP Fusion and 48MP with Ultra Wide and Telephoto capability. The zoom factor is also more impressive with .5, 1x, 2x and 5x. Although you can certainly take macro photos with the iPhone 6, the pro models give you a 48 megapixel experience with macro. That means if you want to take a close-up of a flower or an insect or a beautiful stone, you will get a much higher resolution with the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro models also offer Dolby Vision up to 4K at 120 fps, so if you’d like to make videos, you could shoot a movie in a pretty high resolution. I have seen some amazing videos created by professional filmmakers with just their iPhone 15. So if photography is something you’re interested in then it might be worth investing in one of the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro comes in for storage capacity, choices; 128 GB for $999, 256 GB for $1099, 512 GB for $1299, and one terabyte for $1499. The pro max version comes in only three capacity choices; 256 GB for $1199, 512 GB for $1399 and one terabyte for $1599. Another thing that the prom models have that the base model does not have is what they call ProMotion technology which according to Apple, “ …is a new technology that delivers refresh rates of up to 120Hz for fluid scrolling, greater responsiveness and smoother motion content.” I have only listed a few of the features of these phones, but in real life, most people will be just fine with the iPhone 16. It comes in brighter colors and is slightly more affordable. And the iPhone 16 is the smallest of the new models. But if you travel, and photography is important to you as well as watching movies or video content on your phone, then the iPhone Pro models might be the way to go. Since these are new models, we don’t know if there are any bugs or issues with the hardware. That’s why it’s always prudent to buy AppleCare, or AppleCare plus which includes theft and loss. There are lots of ways to buy these phones, you can buy them directly from Apple, or you can buy them from your cell service provider. Sometimes the cell provider has better deals. You can certainly trade in your iPhone 12, and probably get close to $100 for it from Apple. But you should also check with your cell provider to see if they have promotions. data is very easy if you have backed up your current phone to iCloud. If you haven’t, it’s a good idea to do it before you get a new phone. Your new iPhone can be set up from your iCloud back up or directly from your older phone by having them next to each other. Soon to follow that is a new operating system for the iPhone and iPads. And every year the speed gets better the camera gets better, and hopefully the battery gets better although that hasn’t always been the case. If you are a person who likes to travel and uses your iPhone to take pictures then I would say absolutely, it’s a great idea to upgrade to the new iPhone 16. Of course there are actually four versions of the iPhone 16. There’s the iPhone 16, the 16 Plus, the 16 Pro and the 16 Pro Max. The features between the models and their respective larger versions are not very different, but there are notable differences between the iPhone 16 models and the more expensive and feature-rich Pro models. These are all available for order and will be in stock as of Sept. 20. iPhone 16 and 16 Plus: The iPhone 16 has a 6.1-inch display and is the smallest iPhone 16 available. The 16 Plus model has a 6.7 inch display. These iPhones have an aluminum case with a color infused glass back and come in five colors including ultramarine, teal, pink, white and black. The cameras on these models are what Apple calls the Advanced dual-camera system 48MP Fusion 12MP Ultra Wide. They have optical zoom capability at .5, 1x and 2x. This is a much more advanced camera than your iPhone 12 has, but not as advanced as the pro models of the iPhone 16. The iPhone 16 comes in three storage capacity choices; 128 GB for $799, 256 GB for $899 or 512 GB for $1099. The iPhone 16 plus has the same storage capacity choices and is $100 more expensive for each iPhone 16 Pro and 16 Pro Max The Pro models are slightly bigger. The iPhone 16 Pro has a 6.3 inch display, while the 16 Pro Max has a 6.9 inch display. These models have a titanium case with textured matt glass back. They come in four colors; desert titanium, natural titanium, white and black. It’s with the camera on the pro models that we start to see some of the major differences of the pro models to the less expensive iPhone 16 models. In these phones, Apple has included what they call the Pro camera system with 48MP Fusion and 48MP with Ultra Wide and Telephoto capability. The zoom factor is also more impressive with .5, 1x, 2x and 5x. Although you can certainly take macro photos with the iPhone 6, the pro models give you a 48 megapixel experience with macro. That means if you want to take a close-up of a flower or an insect or a beautiful stone, you will get a much higher resolution with the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro models also offer Dolby Vision up to 4K at 120 fps, so if you’d like to make videos, you could shoot a movie in a pretty high resolution. I have seen some amazing videos created by professional filmmakers with just their iPhone 15. So if photography is something you’re interested in then it might be worth investing in one of the pro models. The iPhone 16 Pro comes in for storage capacity, choices; 128 GB for $999, 256 GB for $1099, 512 GB for $1299, and one terabyte for $1499. The pro max version comes in only three capacity choices; 256 GB for $1199, 512 GB for $1399 and one terabyte for $1599. Another thing that the prom models have that the base model does not have is what they call ProMotion technology which according to Apple, “ …is a new technology that delivers refresh rates of up to 120Hz for fluid scrolling, greater responsiveness and smoother motion content.” I have only listed a few of the features of these phones, but in real life, most people will be just fine with the iPhone 16. It comes in brighter colors and is slightly more affordable. And the iPhone 16 is the smallest of the new models. But if you travel, and photography is important to you as well as watching movies or video content on your phone, then the iPhone Pro models might be the way to go. Since these are new models, we don’t know if there are any bugs or issues with the hardware. That’s why it’s always prudent to buy AppleCare, or AppleCare plus which includes theft and loss. There are lots of ways to buy these phones, you can buy them directly from Apple, or you can buy them from your cell service provider. Sometimes the cell provider has better deals. You can certainly trade in your iPhone 12, and probably get close to $100 for it from Apple. But you should also check with your cell provider to see if they have promotions. By the way, transferring your data is very easy if you have backed up your current phone to iCloud. If you haven’t, it’s a good idea to do it before you get a new phone. Your new iPhone can be set up from your iCloud back up or directly from your older phone by having them next to each other. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, September 18, 2024 City Council Q&A Continued from page 1 the League of Women Voters to advocate for sound city policies in Piedmont. I care deeply about our community and the issues that face our city. I’d like to think one day, one of my kids might come back to raise a family here. I’d like to leave Piedmont better than I found it – a tall order, I know. James Green, Candidate Politics in our country over the last few years has become divisive, contentious, and – at times – dangerous. Over the last three decades serving in the Federal Government and working on public policy in the Bay Area, Washington DC, and overseas, I have been fortunate enough to work with national leaders like Secretary Madeleine Albright and Governor Gary Locke. What I learned was how to listen, how to disagree without being disagreeable, how to lead when times get tough. In essence, what our system of representative democracy should do: elect leaders to improve people’s lives, better the environment, and care for those in need. What inspired me to run for Piedmont City Council is watching our students – including my 7th grader – walk up and down Oakland Ave. to school every morning. I want to bring those lessons of policymaking and politics learned over 30 years to the service of the residents of Piedmont – to help lay the groundwork for the next generation to enjoy an increasingly diverse community, a safe place to learn and play, and a healthy planet. And to show that Piedmont can be a leading example in politics, as it already is in many other areas. Nancy Bostrom, Candidate [No response.] This question was sent to the candidates on Thursday, September 12 via email.
